fields.expected: The hardest one was estimating sleep without a wearable for ClarityAtlas, the iOS health product I built as technical lead at Open Health Intelligence. Most sleep tracking assumes a watch or ring. Our users had phones. I had to infer sleep and wake periods from indirect signals: phone-interaction patterns, plus HealthKit and Core Motion inputs like step count, gait speed, and movement. The problem was that none of those signals tell you someone is asleep. They tell you nobody is moving the phone, which is also true when someone leaves it on a desk. I spent most of the effort on separating those cases and on deciding how much confidence the app should claim, because a health product that confidently reports a wrong sleep window is worse than one that says it isn't sure. I also built the backend for behavioral comparison, including a "Sleep Twins" matching system using standardized behavioral features and weighted distance, which only works if the underlying sleep estimates are stable enough to compare across users. We shipped it into a live pilot at Hopkins with 30+ users, which is where I found most of the failure modes I hadn't anticipated.

fields.expected: During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Ron Daniels was somewhere nearby. We tracked him to Garland Hall, saw him through the locked doors, and knocked until someone let us make the case for what we were building. That turned into a formal meeting months later with him and leadership from the Hopkins Data Science and AI Institute. I'm proud of it less because of who was in the room and more because of what it corrected in me. I had spent most of my time up to that point assuming the technical work was the hard part and that institutional attention would follow good software. It doesn't. Recruiting users, finding the right people to talk to, and repeatedly explaining why something should exist turned out to matter as much as anything I wrote in Swift. Knocking on a locked door is a small thing, but it's the version of initiative I keep having to relearn: the meeting you want usually isn't scheduled, and nobody is going to schedule it for you.

fields.expected: Forward Deployed Software Engineer. The work I've found most useful has always involved a real institution with real constraints rather than a clean problem statement. At Intelehealth I built a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages, combining facility-tier classification, geospatial distance, Google Maps data, weather, and healthcare-resource availability. None of that was interesting as pure modeling. It was interesting because the output had to be usable for care decisions in places where the nearest facility and whether the road is passable actually determine what happens to a patient. Same pattern with ClarityAtlas: I built it end to end, but the part that taught me the most was shipping it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users and finding out which assumptions didn't survive contact with them. I also care about where automation should stop, not just where it can go. On my job-application agent I architecturally prevented free-text and demographic fields from being auto-filled, because a wrong action there has real consequences for a real person. That instinct about the boundary between machine action and human judgment seems more relevant deployed alongside users than at a distance from them.
